items.stem: For a reaction to happen, particles must …
items.answer: collide with enough energy
items.markingKey: Only collisions with enough energy are successful.

items.stem: Why did dark peppered moths become more common in polluted areas in the 1800s?
options: They were better camouflaged on soot-blackened trees, so fewer were eaten
Pale moths moved to the cities
items.answer: They were better camouflaged on soot-blackened trees, so fewer were eaten
items.markingKey: Birds ate more pale moths, so dark moths survived and bred.

items.stem: Explain why the Sun’s energy reaches the Earth by radiation and not by conduction or convection.
items.answer: Space is a vacuum with no particles, so conduction and convection cannot happen; radiation needs no medium.
items.markingKey: space is a vacuum / no particles [1]; radiation needs no medium [1] [2]

items.stem: The Atlantic Ocean is widening at about 2.5 cm per year. What is the distance moved in 1 million years in km?
items.answer: 25 km

items.stem: In a test, Freya writes: "Group 1 metals are hard and dense like iron." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Group 1 metals are soft (can be cut with a knife) and have low densities; lithium, sodium and potassium float on water.
items.markingKey: soft [1]; low density [1] [2]

items.stem: Scientists model the carbon flows in a grassland region each year (thousand tonnes of carbon): photosynthesis removes 200; respiration by plants and animals releases 90; decomposition releases 90; combustion of fuels releases 30. Calculate the net change in carbon in the atmosphere each year.
items.answer: +10 thousand tonnes (increases)
items.markingKey: released = 90 + 90 + 30 = 210 [1]; net = 210 − 200 = 10 thousand tonnes [1] [2]

items.stem: Why is excess copper carbonate added when making copper sulfate?
options: To make sure all the acid is used up
To produce more carbon dioxide gas
items.answer: To make sure all the acid is used up
items.markingKey: Excess solid guarantees no acid is left; the excess is then filtered off.

items.stem: Arjun claims: "Faeces are an example of excretion." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Faeces are mostly undigested food that never entered cells, so their removal is egestion, not excretion.
items.markingKey: faeces = egestion [1]; excretion is waste of metabolism [1] [2]

items.stem: A radio normally takes a current of 0.5 A. Fuses of 1 A, 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Choose the best fuse and explain your choice.
items.answer: 1 A: it is the smallest rating above 0.5 A, so it will not blow in normal use but will blow in a fault.
items.markingKey: 1 A [1]; just above normal current [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq claims: "The balance reading falls because the marble disappears and mass is destroyed." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Mass is conserved; it falls because carbon dioxide gas escapes from the flask.
items.markingKey: mass conserved [1]; gas escapes [1] [2]

items.stem: A body cell of a garden pea has 14 chromosomes. (a) State the number of pairs of chromosomes. (b) State the number in a gamete. (c) Explain why gametes must have half the number of chromosomes.
items.answer: (a) 7 pairs (b) 7 (c) At fertilisation two gametes fuse, so the fertilised egg gets the full number (14) and the number stays the same each generation.
items.markingKey: (a) 7 [1] (b) 7 [1] (c) fusion restores full number [1] [3]

items.stem: Hana carefully pours three liquids, one at a time, down the side of a tall jar so that they form separate layers: golden syrup (density 1.38 g/cm³), washing-up liquid (density 1.06 g/cm³), vegetable oil (density 0.92 g/cm³). List the liquids from the bottom layer to the top layer and explain the order.
items.answer: golden syrup, washing-up liquid, vegetable oil; the densest liquid sinks to the bottom and the least dense floats on top.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; density explanation [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia says: "The planets formed first and then the Sun formed in the middle." Explain why Sofia is wrong.
items.answer: The Sun formed first at the centre of the collapsing cloud; planets formed later from the leftover disc of material.
items.markingKey: Sun forms first [1]; planets from leftover disc [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel reads that diamond is used for the tips of drill bits, while graphite is used for electrodes in electrolysis. (a) Explain why graphite is suitable for electrodes in electrolysis. (b) Explain why a simple molecular substance such as wax would be unsuitable for this work. (c) Suggest one property, other than melting point, that should be tested before choosing a material.
items.answer: (a) It conducts electricity and has a very high melting point. (b) It has a low melting point and is soft, because only weak forces act between its molecules. (c) Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) low melting point / soft [1]; weak forces between molecules [1] [2] (c) valid property with reason [1]; Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia grows tomato plants in water tanks in a greenhouse in Toronto. A concentrated mineral feed containing nitrate and magnesium ions is diluted at 4 cm³ per litre of water. (a) Suggest why air is bubbled through the solution around the roots. (b) Give two reasons why the plants also need water from the solution. (c) Suggest one advantage of growing crops this way in a crowded city.
items.answer: (a) Root cells need oxygen for respiration, to release energy for absorbing mineral ions. (b) Water is a reactant in photosynthesis; it keeps cells firm for support (and carries mineral ions). (c) Mineral supply can be controlled exactly so growth is fast; needs little land (can be stacked or on rooftops) and uses less water.
items.markingKey: (a) oxygen for respiration [1]; energy for root cells / uptake [1] [2] (b) any two reasons [1] each [2] (c) valid advantage [1] with reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi adds 1.5 g of zinc to 50 cm³ of hydrochloric acid until the fizzing stops. 0.15 g of zinc is left unreacted. (a) Write the word equation for the reaction. (b) Explain why excess metal is used. (c) Describe how to remove the unreacted metal. (d) Describe the test for the gas given off and the result.
items.answer: (a) zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen (b) To make sure all the acid reacts, so the salt solution contains no leftover acid. (c) Filter the mixture; the metal stays on the filter paper and the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. (d) Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube: a squeaky pop shows hydrogen.
items.markingKey: (a) zinc chloride [1]; hydrogen [1] [2] (b) all acid used up [1]; pure salt solution [1] [2] (c) filtration [1]; metal residue, salt in filtrate [1] [2] (d) lighted splint [1]; squeaky pop [1] [2]

items.stem: Noah stands two white carnation stems in water containing blue dye, one in a warm, bright, breezy room and one in a cool, dark room. After 20 minutes the dye has risen 42 mm in the first and 17 mm in the second. (a) Calculate the rate of movement in each stem. (b) Name the tissue the dye moves through. (c) Explain the difference between the two results.
items.answer: (a) 2.1 and 0.85 mm/min (b) Xylem (c) Conditions in a warm, bright, breezy room increase evaporation of water from the leaves (transpiration), which pulls water up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) xylem [1] (c) more evaporation / transpiration [1] [3]

items.stem: A technician in Colombo tests a resistor and records: 1.5 V: 0.15 A, 3 V: 0.3 A, 4.5 V: 0.45 A, 6 V: 0.6 A. (a) Predict the current at 9 V. (b) Draw or describe the circuit used. (c) Explain why a filament lamp would not give a straight-line graph.
items.answer: (a) 0.9 A (b) Cell (variable supply) in series with the resistor and an ammeter; voltmeter connected in parallel across the resistor. (c) As the current increases the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases, so current rises less than proportionally.
items.markingKey: (a) I = 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9 A: 0.9 A [1] (b) ammeter in series [1]; voltmeter in parallel [1] [2] (c) filament heats [1]; resistance increases [1] [2]

items.stem: A cube of calcium carbonate has sides of 3 cm. It is cut into 27 identical smaller cubes, each with sides of 1 cm. (a) Calculate the surface area of the large cube. (b) Calculate the total surface area of all the small cubes. (c) Explain how this affects the rate of reaction with acid.
items.answer: (a) 54 cm² (b) 27 × 6 × 1² = 162 cm² (3 times larger) (c) Larger surface area exposes more particles, so collisions are more frequent and the reaction is faster.
items.markingKey: (a) 54 [1] (b) method [1]; 162 cm² [1] (c) more collisions / faster [1] [4]

items.stem: Isla studies birth records for a town: of 2400 babies born, 1236 were boys. (a) Suggest why the numbers are not exactly 50% boys and 50% girls. (b) Describe what happens at fertilisation.
items.answer: (a) Fertilisation is random (chance), so small differences from the expected ratio occur, especially in small samples. (b) The nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an egg, giving a fertilised egg with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
items.markingKey: (a) chance / random [1]; sample size [1] [2] (b) nuclei fuse [1]; 46 / 23 pairs [1] [2]

items.stem: A car engine in a home in Singapore is supplied with 1000 J of energy. 300 J is transferred usefully as kinetic energy. (a) Calculate the energy wasted. (b) Draw or describe an energy flow (Sankey) diagram for the device. (c) Explain how the total energy output compares with the energy supplied.
items.answer: (a) 700 J (b) An arrow 1000 J wide splitting into a useful arrow of 300 J (kinetic energy) and a wasted arrow of 700 J; widths in proportion. (c) They are equal: energy is conserved, so useful + wasted = input.
items.markingKey: (a) 1000 − 300 = 700 J: 700 J [1] (b) input splits into useful and wasted [1]; widths in proportion and labelled [1] [2] (c) equal [1]; conservation of energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya records a 256 Hz note from a keyboard on an oscilloscope set to 2 ms per division. (a) Calculate the period of the sound wave in milliseconds. (b) Calculate how many divisions one complete wave covers on the screen. (c) Explain how the sound travels from the source to the microphone.
items.answer: (a) 3.91 ms (b) 1.95 divisions (c) The source vibrates and pushes on air particles, creating compressions and rarefactions that pass through the air as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 1/256 s [1] = 3.91 ms [1] [2] (b) 3.91 ÷ 2 = 1.95: 1.95 divisions [1] (c) vibrations passed through air particles [1]; compressions and rarefactions [1] [2]

items.stem: What does the temperature of a substance tell us about its particles?
options: How far apart the particles are
How fast they are moving on average
items.answer: How fast they are moving on average
items.markingKey: Higher temperature = greater average kinetic energy of particles.

items.stem: Which is a likely effect of climate change?
options: A fall in average global temperature
items.answer: Rising sea levels
items.markingKey: Warming melts land ice and expands sea water, so sea levels rise.

items.stem: Hana says: "The planets formed first and then the Sun formed in the middle." Explain why Hana is wrong.
items.answer: The Sun formed first at the centre of the collapsing cloud; planets formed later from the leftover disc of material.
items.markingKey: Sun forms first [1]; planets from leftover disc [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid and collects the hydrogen in a gas syringe: 0 s: 0 cm³, 15 s: 42 cm³, 30 s: 55 cm³, 45 s: 58 cm³, 60 s: 60 cm³, 75 s: 60 cm³, 90 s: 60 cm³. What is the mean rate of reaction over the first 15 s?
items.answer: 2.8 cm³/s

items.stem: In a test, Daniel writes: "Water enters a plant through its leaves." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Water is absorbed mainly through the root hair cells; leaves lose water through stomata.
items.markingKey: root hairs absorb water [1]; leaves lose water [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq is designing the circuit for a set of decorative lights for a festival, using a battery, 2 lamps and switches. Describe the circuit, including where the switches go, so that each lamp can be controlled separately and all lamps can be turned off at once.
items.answer: Connect the 2 lamps in parallel, each branch with its own switch; put a master switch in the main circuit next to the battery.
items.markingKey: lamps in parallel [1]; switch on each branch [1] [2]

items.stem: How does the reactivity of Group 1 metals change down the group?
items.answer: It increases
items.markingKey: Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs in reactivity.

items.stem: Arjun claims: "All variation is caused by genes." Do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: No. Variation can be caused by genes, by the environment (e.g. scars, language) or by both (e.g. height, mass).
items.markingKey: environmental causes exist [1]; example [1] [2]

items.stem: Balance this equation: Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
items.answer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
items.markingKey: correct numbers in front of formulae [1]; atoms equal on both sides [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the heating element of an electric kettle is at the bottom.
items.answer: Water heated at the bottom becomes less dense and rises, setting up convection currents that heat all the water.
items.markingKey: heated water rises [1]; convection heats whole kettle [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf investigates how light intensity affects photosynthesis in Canadian pondweed. With a lamp 10 cm away, 60 bubbles are counted in 5 minutes; with the lamp 30 cm away, 12 bubbles are counted in 5 minutes. (a) Name the gas in the bubbles. (b) Name two variables that should be kept the same and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) Temperature of the water and the same piece of plant (or amount of carbon dioxide); so that only light intensity affects the rate (fair test).
items.markingKey: (a) Oxygen [1] (b) two control variables [1]; fair test reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Some scientists once supported the capture theory: the Moon formed elsewhere and was captured by Earth’s gravity. Most scientists now support the collision theory. Describe the collision theory.
items.answer: About 4.5 billion years ago a Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the young Earth; material from the outer layers was thrown into orbit and clumped together to form the Moon.
items.markingKey: Mars-sized body hits Earth [1]; debris orbits and forms Moon [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Isla writes: "Powder gives off more gas in total than chips." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: With the same mass and excess acid, both give the same total volume; powder just produces it faster.
items.markingKey: same total [1]; faster [1] [2]

items.stem: Tomás coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 36 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2.4 g → 1.58 g; B (upper surface coated): 2.8 g → 2.07 g; C (lower surface coated): 2.4 g → 2.11 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2 g → 1.94 g. (a) Calculate the percentage loss in mass of leaf B. (b) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass. (c) Name the process by which the leaves lose mass. (d) Predict how the results would change if the leaves were hung in front of a fan, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) 26.1% (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating. (c) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour). (d) All uncoated surfaces would lose mass faster, because moving air removes water vapour and steepens the gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.8 − 2.07) ÷ 2.8 × 100 [1] = 26.1% [1] [2] (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating [1] (c) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour) [1] (d) faster loss [1]; vapour removed [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia connects different lengths of nichrome wire to a 1.5 V cell and measures the current: 50 cm: 0.15 A, 100 cm: 0.075 A, 150 cm: 0.05 A, 200 cm: 0.0375 A. (a) Calculate the resistance of each length. (b) Describe the relationship between length and resistance. (c) Predict the resistance of a 100 cm length. (d) State two variables that must be kept the same.
items.answer: (a) 50 cm: 10 Ω, 100 cm: 20 Ω, 150 cm: 30 Ω, 200 cm: 40 Ω (b) Resistance is directly proportional to length (doubling length doubles resistance). (c) 20 Ω (d) Thickness and material of the wire, temperature, voltage of cell (any two).
items.markingKey: (a) resistances [1] (b) proportional [1] (c) 20 Ω [1] (d) two variables [1] [4]

items.stem: An engineering company in Lagos uses silicon dioxide (sand) for making glass and graphite for a lubricant in machinery. (a) Explain why silicon dioxide (sand) is suitable for making glass. (b) Explain why graphite is suitable for a lubricant in machinery. (c) Explain why a simple molecular substance such as wax would be unsuitable for this work. (d) Suggest one property, other than melting point, that should be tested before choosing a material.
items.answer: (a) It has a giant covalent structure and a high melting point, so glass is hard and heat-resistant. (b) Its layers slide easily. (c) It has a low melting point and is soft, because only weak forces act between its molecules. (d) Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches.
items.markingKey: (a) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (b) property [1]; linked to structure [1] [2] (c) low melting point / soft [1]; weak forces between molecules [1] [2] (d) valid property with reason [1]; Hardness, electrical conductivity, cost, or how it reacts with substances it touches [1] [2]

items.stem: Records at a hospital in Riyadh show 1500 births in one year: 798 boys and 702 girls. (a) Suggest why the numbers are not exactly 50% boys and 50% girls. (b) Describe what happens at fertilisation.
items.answer: (a) Fertilisation is random (chance), so small differences from the expected ratio occur, especially in small samples. (b) The nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an egg, giving a fertilised egg with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
items.markingKey: (a) chance / random [1]; sample size [1] [2] (b) nuclei fuse [1]; 46 / 23 pairs [1] [2]

items.stem: An engineer in Mumbai is choosing metals for different jobs using the reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, copper, silver, gold. (a) Explain why the copper sulfate solution must not be stored in a tank made of iron. (b) Explain why potassium must never be used in contact with water. (c) Explain why gold is used for electrical contacts in computers even though it is expensive.
items.answer: (a) Iron is more reactive than copper, so it would displace copper and the tank would be eaten away. (b) It is at the top of the series and reacts violently with water, producing hydrogen that can ignite. (c) It is very unreactive, so it does not corrode and keeps a good electrical contact.
items.markingKey: (a) iron more reactive [1]; displaces copper / tank corrodes [1] [2] (b) very reactive [1]; violent reaction / hydrogen [1] [2] (c) unreactive / no corrosion [1]; reliable contact [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho places two thermometers in a room at 28 °C. The bulb of thermometer B is wrapped in cotton wool soaked in ethanol; thermometer A is dry. After 5 minutes A reads 28 °C and B reads 23 °C. A fan is then switched on and B falls to 19 °C. (a) Explain why thermometer B reads lower than A. (b) Explain why the fan lowers the reading further. (c) Explain why thermometer A is included. (d) Predict, with a reason, how the result would change in very humid air.
items.answer: (a) Evaporation from the wet cotton removes the most energetic particles, so energy is taken from the bulb. (b) The fan carries vapour away so evaporation is faster. (c) It is a control, showing the room temperature. (d) B would fall less, because humid air slows evaporation.
items.markingKey: (a) evaporation removes energy [1] (b) faster evaporation [1] (c) control / comparison [1] (d) less cooling with reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Sofia uses hydrogencarbonate indicator, which is red at normal carbon dioxide levels, yellow when carbon dioxide increases and purple when carbon dioxide decreases. Each sealed tube contains indicator: tube A contains a piece of pondweed wrapped in foil (dark); tube B contains nothing (a control) in bright light; tube C contains a small water snail wrapped in foil (dark). The tubes are left for 4 hours. (a) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube A and explain your prediction. (b) Predict the colour of the indicator in tube C and explain your prediction.
items.answer: (a) Yellow: no photosynthesis, but respiration adds carbon dioxide. (b) Yellow: the snail respires, adding carbon dioxide.
items.markingKey: (a) yellow [1]; reason [1] [2] (b) yellow [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined. Evidence includes: (i) fossils of the fern Glossopteris are found in India, Africa, Australia and Antarctica; (ii) rock layers and mountain ranges in Scotland match those in eastern Canada. (a) Explain how evidence (i) supports continental drift. (b) Explain how evidence (ii) supports continental drift. (c) Explain why many scientists rejected Wegener’s idea at first.
items.answer: (a) Its heavy seeds could not cross oceans, so these continents were once joined. (b) The matching rocks formed together before the continents separated. (c) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism.
items.markingKey: (a) valid reasoning about the evidence [1]; so the continents were once joined / have moved [1] [2] (b) valid reasoning about the evidence [1]; so the continents were once joined / have moved [1] [2] (c) He could not explain how continents could move; there was no known mechanism [1]

items.stem: Ethan has hydrochloric acid of concentration 1 mol/dm³. To make weaker solutions, the acid is mixed with water so that the total volume is always 40 cm³. A 2 cm strip of magnesium is added to each mixture and the time for fizzing to stop is recorded: 40 cm³ acid + 0 cm³ water: 29 s, 30 cm³ acid + 10 cm³ water: 37 s, 20 cm³ acid + 20 cm³ water: 54 s, 10 cm³ acid + 30 cm³ water: 109 s. (a) Calculate the concentration of the mixture with 30 cm³ of acid. (b) Describe the pattern in the results. (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model. (d) Explain why the total volume is kept constant.
items.answer: (a) 0.75 mol/dm³ (b) The more concentrated the acid, the shorter the time (faster reaction). (c) More acid particles per cm³ collide with the magnesium more often. (d) So only the concentration changes; it is a fair test.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.75 [1] (b) higher concentration, shorter time [1] (c) more frequent collisions [1] (d) fair test [1] [4]

items.stem: Why does concentrated acid react faster with magnesium than dilute acid?
options: Acid particles collide with the magnesium more often
items.answer: Acid particles collide with the magnesium more often
items.markingKey: Higher concentration → higher collision frequency.

items.stem: Which two elements make up most of a nebula?
items.answer: Hydrogen and helium
items.markingKey: About three-quarters hydrogen and a quarter helium by mass.

items.stem: Elena says: "Giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves, and their babies were born with longer necks." Explain why Elena is wrong.
items.answer: Characteristics acquired during life are not inherited; giraffes with genes for longer necks survived and passed those genes on.
items.markingKey: acquired features not inherited [1]; selection of genetic variation [1] [2]

items.stem: The table shows the mean concentration of carbon dioxide in the air measured at an observatory: 1960: 317 ppm, 1970: 326 ppm, 1980: 339 ppm, 1990: 354 ppm, 2000: 370 ppm, 2010: 390 ppm, 2020: 414 ppm. By how much did the concentration increase between 1990 and 2000?
items.answer: 16 ppm

items.stem: Explain why safety machines such as paper guillotines need two buttons pressed at the same time.
items.answer: The buttons are in series, so the machine works only when both are pressed; the operator’s hands are kept away from the blade.
items.markingKey: series switches [1]; both hands away from blade [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho fixes a drawing pin with wax to the end of rods of different metals, all the same length and thickness. The other ends are heated equally. Times for the pins to fall: iron 60 s, steel 96 s, brass 44 s, copper 12 s. Put the metals in order from best to worst conductor and explain how you decided.
items.answer: copper, brass, iron, steel; the shorter the time for the pin to fall, the faster energy is conducted.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; shorter time = better conductor [1] [2]

items.stem: What does the 2 in 2H₂O mean?
items.answer: Two molecules of water
items.markingKey: The large number in front multiplies the whole formula.

items.stem: In a test, Tomás writes: "Urine is made in the bladder." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: Urine is made in the kidneys; the bladder only stores it.
items.markingKey: made in kidneys [1]; bladder stores [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom of fluorine (F) has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom.
items.answer: 9 protons, 10 neutrons, 9 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = electrons = 9 [1]; neutrons = 19 − 9 = 10 [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Sipho writes: "Raising the temperature increases the amount of product made." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: It increases the rate; the amount of product depends on the amount of reactants.
items.markingKey: rate not amount [1]; amount set by reactants [1] [2]

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit a 1700 Hz note in step. Point X is 5 m from one speaker and 5.4 m from the other. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.) (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Calculate the path difference at X and state how many wavelengths it is. (c) Predict whether X is a loud or a quiet spot.
items.answer: (a) 0.2 m (b) 5.4 − 5 = 0.4 m = 2 wavelengths (c) Loud: whole number of wavelengths, waves arrive in step.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.2 m [1] (b) 2 λ [1] (c) loud with reason [1] [3]

items.stem: A body cell of a horse has 64 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in its sperm or egg cells and in a fertilised egg.
items.answer: 32 in a gamete; 64 in a fertilised egg

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why there is more carbon dioxide in the air of a forest at night than in the middle of the day. (b) Explain why the carbon in coal was not part of the carbon cycle for millions of years.
items.answer: (a) At night there is no photosynthesis, but plants and animals still respire, so CO₂ builds up; in daylight photosynthesis removes it. (b) The organisms were buried before they could decay (no decomposers / no oxygen), so their carbon was locked away until the coal is burned.
items.markingKey: (a) no photosynthesis at night [1]; respiration continues adding CO₂ [1] [2] (b) buried without decomposition [1]; carbon stored until combustion [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun connects a motor and a lamp in parallel to a 12 V battery. Ammeter A1 in the lamp branch reads 0.5 A and ammeter A2 in the motor branch reads 0.2 A. (a) Calculate the current drawn from the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the component carrying the larger current. (c) Explain what happens to the current in the other branch if one component is disconnected. (d) Describe where to connect a voltmeter to check the voltage across one component.
items.answer: (a) 0.7 A (b) 24 Ω (c) It stays the same, because its branch still has the full battery voltage. (d) In parallel, directly across that component.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7 A: 0.7 A [1] (b) R = V/I = 12/0.5 [1] = 24 Ω [1] [2] (c) unchanged [1]; same voltage [1] [2] (d) In parallel, directly across that component [1]

items.stem: Yusuf drops a tennis ball from a height of 1.2 m. It bounces back up to 0.84 m. (a) Describe the energy changes from the moment of release to the top of the bounce. (b) The gravitational potential energy is proportional to height. Calculate the percentage of the original energy the ball still has at the top of the bounce. (c) Predict the height of the second bounce if the same fraction of energy is kept.
items.answer: (a) Gravitational potential → kinetic as it falls; at impact some kinetic is dissipated as thermal and sound, and some stored as elastic energy then back to kinetic; kinetic → gravitational potential as it rises. (b) 0.84 ÷ 1.2 × 100 = 70% (c) 0.84 × 0.7 = 0.588 m

items.stem: Aisha adds four metals, W, X, Y and Z, to solutions of each other’s salts. Results: metal W displaced X, Y; metal X displaced Y; metal Y displaced none of the others; metal Z displaced W, X, Y. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) The metals are copper, iron, magnesium, zinc. Suggest which letter is which metal. (c) Explain why the experiment does not need a test of each metal with its own salt. (d) Suggest one other observation, apart from a coating forming, that shows a reaction has happened. (e) Predict whether copper would react with a solution of a magnesium salt.
items.answer: (a) Z > W > X > Y (b) W = zinc; X = iron; Y = copper; Z = magnesium (c) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information. (d) A temperature rise, or a change in the colour of the solution. (e) No: copper is less reactive than magnesium.
items.markingKey: (a) Z > W > X > Y [1]; Z > W > X > Y [1] [2] (b) all correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (c) A metal cannot displace itself, so there would be no reaction and no information [1] (d) A temperature rise, or a change in the colour of the solution [1] (e) no reaction [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: Felix, who is pregnant, asks a nurse in Dhaka how her diet and lifestyle affect her baby. (a) Explain why the leaflet should advise eating foods rich in protein and iron. (b) Name two substances other than nicotine that can cross the placenta and harm the fetus.
items.answer: (a) Protein is needed to build new cells for growth; iron is needed to make haemoglobin for the fetus’s red blood cells. (b) Any two: alcohol, carbon monoxide, some medicines or drugs, some viruses (e.g. rubella).
items.markingKey: (a) protein for growth [1]; iron for haemoglobin [1] [2] (b) any two [1] each [2]

items.stem: Diego is given three mystery elements: X (atomic number 20), Y (atomic number 17) and Z (atomic number 9). (a) Give the electron arrangement of each element. (b) Describe how X and Y bond together and give the formula of the compound.
items.answer: (a) X 2,8,8,2; Y 2,8,7; Z 2,7 (b) X loses 2 electrons to form X²⁺; Y gains 1 to form Y⁻; ionic bonding; formula XY₂.
items.markingKey: (a) all three correct [2]; two correct [1] [2] (b) electron transfer with charges [1]; ionic attraction [1]; XY₂ [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel reacts 5 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid and times how long it takes to collect 80 cm³ of carbon dioxide: large lumps 200 s, small chips 150 s, powder 25 s. (a) Calculate the mean rate for each form. (b) Calculate how many times faster the powder reacts than the lumps. (c) Explain the results using the particle model. (d) Name two variables kept constant.
items.answer: (a) lumps 0.4, chips 0.533, powder 3.2 cm³/s (b) 8 times (c) The powder has the largest surface area, so more particles are exposed and collisions with acid particles are more frequent. (d) Mass of calcium carbonate, volume, concentration and temperature of the acid (any two).
items.markingKey: (a) all three rates [1] (b) 8 [1] (c) surface area → more frequent collisions [1] (d) two variables [1] [4]

items.stem: A music teacher in Jakarta uses a microphone and oscilloscope to show students the note from a tuning fork marked 256 Hz. The time-base is 1 ms per division. (a) Calculate the period of the sound wave in milliseconds. (b) Explain how the sound travels from the source to the microphone.
items.answer: (a) 3.91 ms (b) The source vibrates and pushes on air particles, creating compressions and rarefactions that pass through the air as a longitudinal wave.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 1/f = 1/256 s [1] = 3.91 ms [1] [2] (b) vibrations passed through air particles [1]; compressions and rarefactions [1] [2]

items.stem: Records at a hospital in Toronto show 1500 births in one year: 710 boys and 790 girls. (a) Explain, using a genetic diagram, why about half of babies are boys. (b) Describe what happens at fertilisation.
items.answer: (a) Mother XX makes eggs all X; father XY makes sperm X or Y in equal numbers; fertilisation gives XX : XY = 1 : 1. (b) The nucleus of a sperm fuses with the nucleus of an egg, giving a fertilised egg with 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
items.markingKey: (a) parents XX and XY [1]; gametes [1]; 1 : 1 offspring [1] [3] (b) nuclei fuse [1]; 46 / 23 pairs [1] [2]

items.stem: In a school laboratory in Istanbul, a class adds sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water around some pondweed (Elodea) and counts bubbles for 5 minutes: 60 bubbles with a lamp at 10 cm and 12 bubbles with the lamp at 30 cm. (a) Name the gas in the bubbles. (b) Suggest why sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water. (c) Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) It releases carbon dioxide, so the plant does not run short of carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. (c) 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: (a) Oxygen [1] (b) supplies carbon dioxide [1]; so CO₂ is not in short supply / does not limit the rate [1] [2] (c) correct formulae [1]; correctly balanced [1] [2]
